item.title: Bank deposits hit record $3 trillion, boosted by dollar deposits scheme
item.description: India's banking system deposits reached a record ₹284 trillion in September, aided by the RBI's discounted dollar swap scheme, which attracted around $133 billion in inflows.
item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / Banking / Bank deposits hit record $3 trillion, boosted by dollar deposits scheme

Bank deposits hit record $3 trillion, boosted by dollar deposits scheme India's banking system deposits reached a record ₹284 trillion in September, aided by the RBI's discounted dollar swap scheme, which attracted around $133 billion in inflows.

India's banking system deposits hit a record ₹284 trillion ($2.99 trillion) in September, boosted by the RBI's discounted dollar swap scheme, which attracted around $133 billion in inflows | Representative Image

Reuters 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 15 2026 | 5:52 PM IST

Listen to This Article

India's banking system deposits hit a record high of around 284 trillion rupees ($2.99 trillion) in the second half of September, central bank data showed on Thursday.   Deposits rose by 21.67 trillion rupees in the first six months of the financial year, with most of the increase seen between June and August, when the central bank's discounted swap window to attract dollar inflows was in place.   Banking system deposits jumped by an aggregate of 20 trillion rupees from June 16 to August 31, according to data from the Reserve Bank of India.   In June, the RBI announced a discounted swap window to attract foreign-currency deposits and encouraged lenders to raise cheaper deposits.     The scheme saw inflows of around $133 billion and the deposit window was closed on August 31, a month earlier than planned. Deposits were also boosted by lenders' efforts to build funding buffers before the end of the quarter; the fortnight ended September 30 saw inflows of 7.73 trillion rupees.   Overall deposits in the banking system as of September-end were up 8.4 per cent as compared with March-end. Competition for deposits stayed contained, while the system was in surplus, CareEdge Ratings said in a note.   "The October rate hike rules out further cuts in term deposit rates for now and is likely to push them up, as banks need to fund credit that is growing faster than deposits while the liquidity surplus shrinks," CareEdge added.   More From This Section

Home / World News / Marco Rubio to meet Mukesh Ambani in Jamnagar, says US envoy Sergio Gor

Marco Rubio to meet Mukesh Ambani in Jamnagar, says US envoy Sergio Gor The visit is Rubio's second to India this year after a trip to New Delhi in May

Rubio will travel to Mumbai and Jamnagar as part of a trip that also includes Samarkand, Uzbekistan. (Photo: PTI)

Bloomberg 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 15 2026 | 5:23 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Secretary of State Marco Rubio will travel to India next week for a visit focused on deepening cooperation in energy and spurring investment and economic opportunities.   Rubio will travel to Mumbai and Jamnagar as part of a trip that also includes Samarkand, Uzbekistan, from Oct. 17 to 22, the State Department said in a statement. Mumbai is India's financial capital while Jamnagar, in Gujarat, is home to the world's largest oil refining complex, owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries Ltd.   President Donald Trump's top diplomat "will meet with senior government officials to strengthen the U.S.-India strategic partnership, exchange views on regional and global dynamics, and discuss prospects for enhanced energy cooperation," the State Department said. "Secretary Rubio will also meet with business leaders to promote opportunities for commercial investment and economic cooperation."

The visit is Rubio's second to India this year after a trip to New Delhi in May.   In Uzbekistan, he'll take part in meetings with counterparts from a grouping that includes Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and the Kyrgyz Republic - known as C5+1 - focused on promoting regional peace and prosperity. He'll also lead a delegation of more than 200 US business leaders focused on strengthening cooperation.

Home / India News / Vijay Mallya's flamboyant lifestyle delaying loan settlement: Karnataka HC

Vijay Mallya's flamboyant lifestyle delaying loan settlement: Karnataka HC The court made the observation while granting relief to Diageo Holdings Netherlands BV in a dispute over shares held by Mallya in UBL

Vijay Mallya (REUTERS/File Photo)

Vrinda Goel New Delhi 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 15 2026 | 4:36 PM IST

Listen to This Article

The Karnataka High Court on Wednesday observed that former Kingfisher Airlines promoter Vijay Mallya’s “flamboyant lifestyle” appeared to be hindering the closure of loan recovery proceedings pending against the now-defunct airline, Bar and Bench reported.   A Division Bench made the observation while granting relief to Diageo Holdings Netherlands BV in a dispute over shares held by Mallya in United Breweries Limited (UBL), which had been pledged in connection with a loan.   The Bench noted that even decades of work could be undone when the focus shifted from operational excellence and financial prudence to “personal vanity, outsized egos and hedonistic excess”. The court said that when disciplined grit was replaced by a cult of personality and hubris, the result could be bankruptcy and ruin.

Recounting Mallya’s rise in the liquor business and the expansion of his empire, the Bench noted that he came to be known as the “King of Good Times”, with his flamboyant lifestyle becoming inseparable from the brand he built. His “debt-fuelled gamble” on Kingfisher Airlines, however, collapsed, eventually leading to his status as a fugitive economic offender, it added.   “More than anything else, we are also of the view that it is Dr Vijay Mallya’s flamboyant lifestyle, excessive personal indulgence and his personal vanity are coming in the way of giving quietus to the claims of the Consortium of Banks against the loan of ₹6,203 crore advanced to the defunct Kingfisher Airlines Ltd,” the court observed.

Also Read

Jio eyes big share of India's digital economy: Akash Ambani ahead of IPO

Actor Imran Khan asked to leave India: What law says about OCI cardholders

EPFO extends PF filing deadline to Oct 31: What employees should check

Why was IDBI Bank sold at ₹81 a share? Understanding the valuation

The court held that Diageo’s claim ranked higher than the banks’ entitlement to these shares. It also noted that the banks had already recovered assets worth ₹14,131.6 crore against the ₹6,203 crore loan extended to Kingfisher Airlines. The court held that the banks were not justified in staking a claim over the UBL shares as well. The Bench added that it was now up to the consortium of banks and the government to close the loan recovery proceedings.   How did Vijay Mallya respond?   Responding to the court’s remarks, Mallya said in a post on X that he was being punished for living a “Kingsize” life with his own money.

“Am I still a Chor or Cheat?” he said. “I lived life Kingsize with my own money and that was my biggest crime for which I am being punished."   Order passed by a Division Bench of the Hon’ble Karnataka High Court. I sincerely request you to read carefully. Am I still a Chor or Cheat ? I lived life Kingsize with my own money and that was my biggest crime for which I am being punished . There is a God above for all of us. Someday Justice will prevail. — Vijay Mallya (@TheVijayMallya) October 14, 2026   What is the case about?   The case before the court concerned UBL shares held by Mallya individually, as well as shares jointly held by him and his son, Sidhartha Mallya, in United Breweries.   Diageo’s claim arose from a $135 million loan that Standard Chartered Bank (SCB) extended to Watson Ltd, an overseas company of Mallya, in July 2013. The loan was secured by a pledge of UBL shares, and Diageo guaranteed it. After Watson defaulted, Diageo paid the bank $140.97 million in January 2016 and claimed to have stepped into SCB’s shoes.

A consortium of banks, however, had obtained certain interim orders in recovery proceedings against Kingfisher Airlines, freezing the shares. The banks argued that the UBL shares could be used to recover the ₹6,203 crore owed to them by Kingfisher Airlines and that Diageo’s pledge over the shares was ineffective.   Mallya and UBL had guaranteed repayment of the loan under a Master Debt Recast Agreement dated December 21, 2010.   Diageo approached the high court for relief after the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) and the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) ruled against it. The high court held that the pledge created in favour of SCB in 2013 had priority over the bank consortium’s claim under the 2010 agreement.

The court also noted that Sidhartha Mallya was not a party to the Master Debt Recast Agreement with the banks. It further held that Mallya’s personal guarantee did not, by itself, create a proprietary charge over the jointly held shares.   Mallya left India in 2016 and lives in the UK. He was declared a fugitive economic offender in 2019, and India has long sought his extradition over alleged loan defaults and money laundering.   More From This Section

Home / World News / IMF chief urges wealthy nations to tackle rising global debt levels

IMF chief urges wealthy nations to tackle rising global debt levels That is forcing countries to make hard choices between supporting their most vulnerable people and meeting their debt repayment obligations

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva | Image: Bloomberg

AP Bangkok 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 14 2026 | 10:08 PM IST

Listen to This Article

The head of the International Monetary Fund said Wednesday that the US and other wealthy nations need to urgently tackle mounting global debt levels that are weighing heaviest on low-income countries and straining the global financial system. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said that while US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other US leaders recognise that the federal deficit and national debt have grown too high, just trying to grow the US economy out of its more than USD 40 trillion in national debt would not suffice. "At the fund, we believe that, growth, of course, helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments," Georgieva said at the autumn meeting of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok.

"There is no magic," she said, noting some other measures would be needed. "You have to go in a direction of tightening that, bringing it down, bringing deficit down." Fiscal consolidation' faces challenges Rising debt levels and global inflation, partly resulting from high energy costs due to the Iran war, have pushed interest rates to multidecade highs, adding to the burdens of the world's poorest nations. Also Read

Best of Opinion: Global growth headline numbers mask vulnerabilities

Global growth resilience premium

AI investment props up global growth, but war, debt threaten outlook: IMF

IMF raises India's growth forecast to 7% in FY27 on strong domestic demand

Global economy nears limits of resilience as energy squeeze persists: IMF

Efforts to bring debt under control with what Georgieva and other experts call "fiscal consolidation" have suffered setbacks from heavy spending during the COVID-19 pandemic and since. "Fiscal risks are rising, and a proper reaction is largely absent in many countries," said Rodrigo Valdes, director of the IMF's Fiscal Affairs Department. "And in major advanced economies, the effect of fiscal indiscipline does not stop at the border. It travels to the rest of the world."   "Among the world's poorest countries, interest payments have reached historic highs relative to revenue, and declining amounts of aid are creating gaps that some countries have been unable to finance," the IMF's latest Fiscal Monitor said.

That is forcing countries to make hard choices between supporting their most vulnerable people and meeting their debt repayment obligations. Nations need help with job creation, investment "We know that today the median developing country is going to pay, is actually today paying three times more on their interest repayments than developed countries," Alexander De Croo, former Belgian prime minister and the administrator of the United Nations Development Programme, said in an interview with The Associated Press. On average nearly 10 per cent of government spending is going to repay debt, and the combination of high prices for fuel, fertiliser and other needs, the impact of the El Nino weather phenomenon and higher borrowing costs has left many low income countries with little opportunity to recover.

"I mean, we don't see really a light at the end of the tunnel," De Croo said. Generating jobs, especially at a time when increasing use of artificial intelligence threatens to make many traditional occupations obsolete, is another top priority. More than 1.2 billion young people are expected to enter the global workforce in the next decade or so, while forecasts suggest a net creation of only 400 million new jobs. The UNDP announced this week a "Jobs for Prosperity" initiative that will work with governments, development banks such as the World Bank and private businesses to encourage investment in key job creating areas such as tourism, healthcare and food processing.

The initiative and other efforts will focus on helping countries attract investment by improving their governance and policies, while creating pipelines of "investible projects," De Croo said. "These are things that are feasible. It's been proven that you can do it in many places of the world.
